title: Linear scan for JIT compilers
hook: Why do JITs use linear scan instead of graph coloring?

scenes.caption: Graph coloring builds a large interference graph and iterates, which costs too much at JIT time.
scenes.narration: Graph coloring builds an interference graph and iterates, costing space and several passes. A JIT pays compile time as user-visible latency.

elements.text: JITs trade some code quality for speed.

scenes.caption: Each value becomes one interval from its first definition to its last use, in linear instruction order.
scenes.narration: Number the instructions linearly. Each virtual register becomes one live interval, from its first definition to its last use, ignoring holes.

scenes.caption: Sweep intervals by start point, expiring finished ones and spilling when all registers are busy.
scenes.narration: Poletto and Sarkar sweep intervals by start. Expire finished ones, assign a free register, and if none is free, spill the active interval ending furthest away.

elements.text: active is kept sorted by end point.

scenes.caption: The trade-off is precision: one coarse interval per value gives worse code than coloring.
scenes.narration: The price is quality. Coarse intervals waste registers in lifetime holes, and spilling a whole interval is blunt. Interval splitting recovers much of the loss.

scenes.caption: HotSpot C1 and V8's TurboFan both allocate registers with linear-scan variants.
scenes.narration: Production JITs make this trade. HotSpot's C1 uses linear scan, and V8's TurboFan has a linear-scan allocator. Ahead-of-time compilers can afford more.

elements.text: Ahead-of-time compilers can spend more time on allocation.

takeaway: Linear scan makes one fast pass over coarse live intervals, trading some code quality for compile time that a JIT cannot afford to waste.
